name: e⁺e⁻ → u ū
explanation: Electron–positron annihilation into a virtual photon that produces a quark–antiquark pair. The ratio of hadron to muon production in such events measures the number of quark colors.

name: u u → u u (gluon exchange)
explanation: Two up quarks scatter by exchanging a virtual gluon, the strong-force analogue of Møller scattering. Each quark keeps its flavor because the gluon couples a quark only to itself.

name: e⁺e⁻ → q q̄ g
explanation: Annihilation produces a quark–antiquark pair, and one of the quarks radiates a gluon. Three-jet events like this gave the first direct evidence for the gluon.

name: Drell–Yan: u ū → μ⁺μ⁻
explanation: A quark from one proton and an antiquark from the other annihilate into a virtual photon, which becomes a muon pair. The clean muon signature makes this a classic probe of proton structure.

name: J/ψ → e⁺e⁻ (c c̄ annihilation)
explanation: The charm–anticharm pair inside a J/ψ annihilates into a virtual photon that becomes an electron–positron pair. This clean leptonic decay made the J/ψ easy to discover in 1974.

name: g g → g g (four-gluon vertex)
explanation: Gluons carry color charge themselves, so they interact directly with each other, including through a four-gluon contact vertex. This self-interaction has no QED analogue and underlies confinement.

name: q q̄ → g g
explanation: A quark and antiquark annihilate into two gluons, with a virtual quark exchanged between the vertices. It is the strong-force counterpart of e⁺e⁻ → γγ.

name: g g → q q̄ (s-channel gluon)
explanation: Two gluons fuse into a virtual gluon through the three-gluon vertex, which then splits into a quark–antiquark pair. Gluon fusion dominates quark production at hadron colliders.

name: Υ → g g g (b b̄ annihilation)
explanation: A bottom–antibottom pair annihilates into three gluons through a chain of virtual bottom quarks. Three gluons are required because color conservation forbids annihilation into just one or two.

name: g g → t t̄
explanation: Two gluons from colliding protons fuse into a virtual gluon that splits into a top–antitop pair. This is the main way top quarks are produced at the LHC.
